p: The Leningrad Codex says Bezalel 'had set' the altar there. Many manuscripts and the Greek say it 'was there.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ('he put')
Many Hebrew manuscripts, as reported; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἐκεῖ); Latin Vulgate; NIV, ESV

why: The two Hebrew words differ only in a dot over one letter (sin or shin). 'He put' is the Leningrad reading and makes good sense: Bezalel set the altar before the tabernacle (Exodus 40:29). 'There' fits the flow of 1:3–6 and is the reading of most translations. The meaning is nearly the same.

a: from the high place at Gibeon
p: The Hebrew says Solomon came 'to' the high place; the Greek and Latin say 'from.'

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἐκ); Latin Vulgate; KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.plain: from the high place at Gibeon

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: to the high place at Gibeon

why: Solomon is leaving Gibeon for Jerusalem, so 'from' must be meant. The Hebrew 'to' is probably a copying slip, though a few scholars think the preposition could carry the sense 'from' in older Hebrew. Almost all translations read 'from.'

a: three thousand six hundred to oversee them
p: Chronicles has 3,600 overseers here and at 2:18. 1 Kings 5:16 has 3,300.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (τρισχίλιοι ἑξακόσιοι)
readings.plain: three thousand six hundred to oversee them

readings.w: 1 Kings 5:16 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: three thousand three hundred to oversee them

readings.w: Some Greek manuscripts of 1 Kings 5:16 (3 Kingdoms 5:30), as reported
readings.plain: three thousand six hundred to oversee them

why: The two books count the officers differently but reach the same total. Kings has 3,300 foremen (1 Kings 5:16) and 550 chiefs (1 Kings 9:23); Chronicles has 3,600 (2:2; 2:18) and 250 (8:10). Both make 3,850. That suggests one body of officers divided in two ways, not a copying error. Some Greek copies of Kings already have 3,600, agreeing with Chronicles.

a: twenty thousand cors of threshed wheat
p: Chronicles' Hebrew has makkot, 'blows,' perhaps 'beaten' wheat. Kings has makkolet, 'food,' and the Greek has 'for food.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: twenty thousand cors of threshed wheat

readings.w: 1 Kings 5:11 (Masoretic Text, מַכֹּלֶת); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (εἰς βρώματα, though attached to the timber)
readings.plain: twenty thousand cors of wheat as food

why: The Hebrew of Chronicles can be read as wheat that has been beaten, that is threshed, and the Plain keeps it. Many scholars think it is a slip for Kings' makkolet, 'food,' which differs by one letter; the Greek of Chronicles has 'for food' in the same verse. The meaning changes little: wheat was paid as food for the workers.

a: in the second month, on its second day
p: The Hebrew dates the start to 'the second month, on the second.' The Greek has only 'the second month.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: in the second month, on the second
readings.plain: in the second month, on its second day

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἐν τῷ μηνὶ τῷ δευτέρῳ); 1 Kings 6:1; many modern versions

why: The second 'second' (bashsheni) may be an accidental repeat of the word just before it, and Kings has only the month. But Hebrew can give a day this way, and the Plain keeps it as 'on its second day.' The meaning is unchanged either way: the work began in spring of Solomon's fourth year.

a: a hundred and twenty cubits high
p: The Hebrew and most Greek copies make the porch 120 cubits high. Some Greek copies and the Syriac have 20.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἑκατὸν εἴκοσι); KJV, ESV
readings.plain: a hundred and twenty cubits high

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and some other Greek manuscripts, and the Syriac Peshitta, as reported; NIV, NRSV

why: The best-supported reading is 120, in the Hebrew and in Rahlfs' Greek. 'Twenty' may be original, but it may also be a copyist's correction of an unlikely height. The Plain keeps the Hebrew; the note on this phrase gives the explanations offered.

p: Chronicles gives the pillars 35 cubits; Kings and Jeremiah give each 18.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (τριάκοντα πέντε)
1 Kings 7:15; Jeremiah 52:21 (Masoretic Text); the Syriac Peshitta of Chronicles, as reported (not checked)

why: All Hebrew and Greek witnesses to Chronicles have thirty-five; the Syriac, as reported, has eighteen, probably brought into line with Kings. So thirty-five is the text of Chronicles, and the Plain translates it. The note on this phrase gives the explanations offered.

t: Chains 'in the inner room' or 'like a necklace'?
p: The Hebrew says he made chains 'in the inner room,' which seems out of place. Many scholars read 'like a necklace.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἐν τῷ δαβιρ); KJV ('as in the oracle')
Scholarly emendation (no manuscript), adopted by the ESV ('like a necklace') and others

why: The chains belong to the pillars outside, so 'in the inner room' is odd. Reading two similar-looking letters differently (kaf for bet, resh for dalet) turns bdbyr into krbyd, 'like a necklace,' a rare word found in Ezekiel 16:11 and Genesis 41:42. No manuscript has it, and the Greek supports the Hebrew. The KJV took the phrase to mean chains like those in the inner room (compare 1 Kings 6:21). The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

p: Chronicles has figures of oxen under the Sea's rim; Kings has gourd shapes. The Hebrew words differ in two letters.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (μόσχων, 'calves')
1 Kings 7:24 (Masoretic Text)

why: All witnesses to Chronicles have 'oxen' (the Greek, checked, has 'calves'), so the Plain translates it. Most scholars think it began as a misreading of Kings' peqa'im, 'gourds': the words share their shape but differ in two letters (bet for pe, resh for ayin), and the twelve oxen of the next verse would make the slip easy. Ten figures to every cubit would also be very small for oxen.

t: Three thousand or two thousand baths?
p: Chronicles gives the Sea a capacity of 3,000 baths; Kings has 2,000.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (τρισχιλίους)
1 Kings 7:26 (Masoretic Text)

why: Chronicles is consistent in all its witnesses. Some scholars think it gives the Sea's full capacity and Kings its usual filling; others that one number is a copying error. The parallel variant at 1 Kings 7:26 keeps Kings' figure there; here the Plain keeps Chronicles'.

p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) spells the craftsman's name Hiram here; the reading tradition (Qere) has Huram.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the reading tradition (Qere)
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the written text (Ketiv); compare 1 Kings 7:40

why: The two spellings are forms of one name. Chronicles elsewhere spells it Huram, and the Masoretes asked readers to say Huram here too; the written Hiram matches Kings. The Plain follows the Qere, as it does at 9:10.

a: the stands he made, and the basins he made on the stands
p: Kings lists 'the ten stands' and 'the ten basins.' The Hebrew of Chronicles has 'he made' twice. The Greek has both.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the stands he made, the basins he made
readings.plain: the stands he made, and the basins he made on the stands

readings.w: 1 Kings 7:43 (Masoretic Text)
readings.en: the ten stands ... the ten basins
readings.plain: the ten stands, with the ten basins on the stands

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org)
readings.en: he made ten stands, and the basins he made on the stands
readings.plain: the ten stands he made, and the basins he made on the stands

why: 'He made' ('asah) and 'ten' ('eser) look alike in Hebrew, and the list form of the verse expects a number, so most scholars think Chronicles' Hebrew has a copying slip. The Greek may combine both readings. The Plain translates the Hebrew; the meaning is the same either way.

t: 'The Levite priests' or 'the priests and the Levites'?
p: The Leningrad Codex has 'the Levite priests.' Kings, many Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek have 'the priests and the Levites.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
1 Kings 8:4; many Hebrew manuscripts, as reported; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (οἱ ἱερεῖς καὶ οἱ Λευῖται); Vulgate; NIV, ESV

why: 'The Levite priests' is Deuteronomy's phrase (Deuteronomy 17:9; 18:1) and may be original, but Chronicles usually distinguishes priests and Levites, and 5:4 has just said the Levites lifted the ark. A missing 'and' (one letter) could explain the Leningrad reading. The Plain keeps the Leningrad text, which still makes sense: priests, who are Levites, carried the holy objects.

a: It has stayed there until today.
p: Chronicles' Hebrew has 'it was there,' perhaps the ark. Kings and the Greek have 'they are there,' the poles.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: It has stayed there until today.

readings.w: 1 Kings 8:8 (Masoretic Text); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἦσαν ἐκεῖ); many Hebrew manuscripts, as reported
readings.plain: They have stayed there until today.

why: The singular could be a slip for the plural of Kings, or a deliberate change that makes the ark, not the poles, the subject. Most translations use the plural. The Plain keeps the Hebrew of Chronicles.

a: Nor did I choose any man to be ruler over my people Israel.
p: Chronicles has two refusals and two choices. Kings lacks the refusal of a ruler and the choice of Jerusalem. Goes with 6:6.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org); probably the Qumran fragment 4QKings, as reconstructed
readings.orig: וְלֹא־בָחַרְתִּי בְאִישׁ לִהְיוֹת נָגִיד עַל־עַמִּי יִשְׂרָאֵל
readings.en: and I did not choose a man to be ruler over my people Israel
readings.plain: Nor did I choose any man to be ruler over my people Israel.

readings.w: 1 Kings 8:16 (Masoretic Text)

why: The full text is balanced: no city and no man before, then Jerusalem and David. A copyist's eye skipping from one 'I chose' to the next would explain the shorter text of Kings. All witnesses to Chronicles have the longer text.
b: See the variant on 1 Kings 8:16 for the evidence in Kings.

a: I chose Jerusalem for my name to be there, and I chose David
p: Kings has only 'I chose David.' Goes with 6:5.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org)
readings.orig: וָאֶבְחַר בִּירוּשָׁלַ‍ִם לִהְיוֹת שְׁמִי שָׁם וָאֶבְחַר בְּדָוִיד
readings.en: and I chose Jerusalem for my name to be there, and I chose David
readings.plain: I chose Jerusalem for my name to be there, and I chose David

readings.w: 1 Kings 8:16 (Masoretic Text)

why: See 6:5. The choice of Jerusalem appears in all witnesses to Chronicles.

a: For Solomon had made a bronze platform and put it in the middle of the courtyard. It was five cubits long, five cubits wide and three cubits high. He stood on it. Then he went down on his knees in front of all the assembly of Israel and lifted his open palms to the heavens.
p: This verse is in Chronicles only. It may have dropped out of Kings, or Chronicles may have added it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (βάσιν χαλκῆν)
readings.en: for Solomon had made a bronze platform ...
readings.plain: For Solomon had made a bronze platform and put it in the middle of the courtyard. It was five cubits long, five cubits wide and three cubits high. He stood on it. Then he went down on his knees in front of all the assembly of Israel and lifted his open palms to the heavens.

readings.w: 1 Kings 8:22–23 (Masoretic Text and Greek)

why: 6:12 and 6:13 both end with the same words, 'and lifted his open palms,' exactly the setting in which a copyist's eye skips a line (homoioteleuton). Many scholars (Rudolph, Williamson) think Kings lost the verse that way; others (Japhet) think Chronicles added it. The verse belongs to Chronicles either way.

p: The Leningrad Codex has the plural. Many Hebrew manuscripts and Psalm 132:10 have the singular.

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts, as reported; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (τοῦ χριστοῦ σου); Psalm 132:10; KJV, NIV, ESV
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)

why: The difference is one letter (yod), the kind of letter often added or dropped in copying. The psalm Chronicles quotes has the singular, and the king praying is one man. The plural could refer to David and Solomon together, and some scholars prefer it as the harder reading. The Plain follows the singular.

p: Chronicles has 250 chief overseers; Kings has 550. Both books' totals of officers come to 3,850.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles
1 Kings 9:23 (Masoretic Text)

why: Kings counts 3,300 foremen plus 550 chiefs; Chronicles 3,600 (2:2; 2:18) plus 250; see the variant on 2:2. The matching total suggests two ways of dividing one body of officers, not a copying error. The written Hebrew (Ketiv) also has 'garrisons' (netsivim) where the reading tradition (Qere) has 'overseers' (nitsavim); the Plain follows the Qere.

a: up to the day the LORD's house was founded
t: 'Up to' or 'from' the day it was founded?
p: The Hebrew reads 'up to the day of the founding.' The Greek reads 'from the day it was founded.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: until the day of the founding
readings.plain: up to the day the LORD's house was founded

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἀφ᾽ ἧς ἡμέρας ἐθεμελιώθη); Syriac and Vulgate, as reported; most modern versions
readings.en: from the day of the founding
readings.plain: from the day the LORD's house was founded

why: 'From the founding until it was finished' reads more smoothly, and many scholars think the Hebrew 'until' was repeated by mistake from the next phrase. The Hebrew can still make sense: everything was prepared up to the laying of the foundation and carried on until the house was done. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

p: Chronicles has 450 talents of gold from Ophir; Kings has 420; the Greek of Kings has 120.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles
1 Kings 9:28 (Masoretic Text)
Septuagint of Kings (3 Kingdoms 9:28), Codex Vaticanus, as reported

why: Numbers are easily miscopied, and none of the three can be shown to be original. The Plain follows Chronicles here, as the Kings page follows Kings.

a: the stairway by which he went up to the LORD's house
p: Chronicles' Hebrew has 'his ascent (or upper room) by which he went up.' Kings and the Greek of Chronicles have 'his burnt offerings.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles
readings.en: and his ascent by which he went up
readings.plain: the stairway by which he went up to the LORD's house

readings.w: 1 Kings 10:5 (Masoretic Text); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) of Chronicles (τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα ἃ ἀνέφερεν)
readings.en: and his burnt offering(s) that he offered up
readings.plain: the burnt offerings he offered up at the LORD's house

why: The two Hebrew words differ by one letter (yod). The Greek of Chronicles agrees with Kings, which suggests 'burnt offerings' was the older text and 'ascent' a slip or a reinterpretation; the verb 'go up' fits both. The Plain translates the Hebrew of Chronicles, which makes sense: Solomon's private stairway to the Temple (compare 2 Kings 16:18).

p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) spells the king's name Hiram here; the reading tradition (Qere) has Huram.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the reading tradition (Qere)
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the written text (Ketiv); compare 1 Kings 10:11

why: As at 4:11, the written text has the Kings spelling and the reading tradition the usual Chronicles spelling. The Plain follows the Qere in both places, so the king is Huram throughout Chronicles' own verses.

a: and a footstool of gold was fastened to the throne
t: A footstool, a round top, or a calf's head?
p: Chronicles has a gold footstool; Kings has a round top or calf's head; the Greek of Chronicles has steps 'bound with gold.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles
readings.en: and a footstool in gold, fastened to the throne
readings.plain: and a footstool of gold was fastened to the throne

readings.w: 1 Kings 10:19 (Masoretic Text)
readings.en: and a round top to the throne behind it
readings.plain: and behind it, the throne had a round top

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) of Chronicles

why: The three readings may all come from one damaged phrase. Kings' Greek ('calves' heads') suggests 'egel, 'calf,' behind 'agol, 'round'; Chronicles' kevesh, 'footstool,' and the Greek's 'bound' may reflect other readings of the same letters. The Plain translates Chronicles' Hebrew.

p: Chronicles says the ships went to Tarshish; Kings speaks of 'Tarshish ships,' a type of vessel.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἐπορεύετο εἰς Θαρσις)
1 Kings 10:22 (Masoretic Text)

why: All witnesses to Chronicles read a destination, so the Plain translates it. Most scholars think Chronicles reinterpreted Kings' term for a type of ship; see the note.

t: Four thousand or forty thousand stalls?
p: Chronicles has four thousand stalls; 1 Kings 4:26 has forty thousand.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) ('four thousand mares for chariots')
1 Kings 4:26 (Masoretic Text)

why: Chronicles and its Greek agree on four thousand; the Greek takes the word as mares rather than stalls. The Plain follows Chronicles here, as the Kings page follows Kings; the note on this phrase discusses which figure is likelier.

p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) spells the seer's name Yedi; the reading tradition (Qere) Yedo, 'Iddo.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the reading tradition (Qere); KJV, NIV, ESV
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the written text (Ketiv)

why: The two spellings differ by the small letters yod and vav, often confused. The Plain follows the Qere, Ye'do, but prints it as 'Iddo,' the spelling of the same seer's name in 12:15 and 13:22 ('Iddo); this normalizes the name to those verses and to the usual English form.

t: Came back from Egypt, or lived in Egypt?
p: Chronicles' vowels read 'returned from Egypt'; Kings' read 'lived in Egypt.' The consonants of the verb are the same.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ἀπέστρεψεν ... ἐξ Αἰγύπτου)
1 Kings 12:2 (Masoretic Text)

why: Chronicles has 'from Egypt' (mimmitsrayim), which requires 'returned.' Kings has 'in Egypt' (bemitsrayim), which goes with 'lived.' Many scholars think Kings once also read 'returned from Egypt,' which fits Jeroboam's presence at Shechem in the next verse.

a: Be kind to this people, show them favor
p: Chronicles: 'If you are good to this people.' Kings: 'If you become a servant to this people today.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Chronicles
readings.en: if you are for good to this people and please them
readings.plain: Be kind to this people, show them favor

readings.w: 1 Kings 12:7 (Masoretic Text)
readings.en: if today you become a servant to this people and serve them
readings.plain: Become a servant to this people today and serve them

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) of Chronicles
readings.en: if today you become good to this people
readings.plain: Be kind to this people today, show them favor

why: Chronicles' Hebrew is supported by its Greek, which also keeps Kings' 'today,' so the change is old and probably the Chronicler's own. The Plain follows Chronicles' Hebrew. See the note.

a: My father made your yoke heavy
t: 'My father made heavy' or 'I will make heavy'?
p: The Leningrad Codex reads 'I will make your yoke heavy.' Kings, many manuscripts and the Greek read 'My father made your yoke heavy.'

readings.w: 1 Kings 12:14; many Hebrew manuscripts, as reported; Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (ὁ πατήρ μου ἐβάρυνεν); KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.en: my father made your yoke heavy
readings.plain: My father made your yoke heavy

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: I will make your yoke heavy
readings.plain: I will make your yoke heavy

why: The Leningrad reading can be explained as a copying slip: avi hikhbid, 'my father made heavy,' lost a few letters (bet, yod and he) and became akhbid, 'I will make heavy.' The longer reading matches 10:10–11, Kings and the Greek. The Plain follows it, as most translations do.

p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) says Mahalath was the 'son' of Jerimoth; the reading tradition (Qere) corrects it to 'daughter.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the reading tradition (Qere); Septuagint, Rahlfs' edition (checked at blueletterbible.org) (θυγατέρα); all English versions
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the written text (Ketiv)

why: Mahalath is a woman's name and Rehoboam takes her as his wife, so 'son' must be a slip, perhaps caught from 'son of David' a few words later. The Masoretes marked the correction.
